title: Intent: Abstract Factory
body: Provide an interface for creating families of related objects without specifying concrete classes.

title: Use Abstract Factory when
body: A system must produce compatible sets of components (UI widgets, storage clients, drivers) that vary by environment but must work together.

title: Trade-off: Abstract Factory
body:
**Benefit**: Enforces consistency among related products and centralizes family selection.

**Cost**: Adding a new product kind requires changing every factory interface and implementation.

title: Q1: Abstract Factory differs from Factory Method because it:
body:
A. Creates one product via inheritance hook only
B. Creates families of related products together
C. Clones existing instances
D. Builds objects step by step

**B.** Its focus is consistent families (e.g., queue + storage + metrics) per environment.

title: Q2: When adding a new product type to an Abstract Factory, you u
body:
A. Change only one concrete class
B. Update all factory interfaces and concrete factories
C. Add a database migration
D. Introduce an event bus

**B.** The abstraction declares creation for every family member, so it widens across implementations.

title: Intent: Adapter
body: Convert the interface of a component into one clients expect so incompatible interfaces can collaborate.

title: Use Adapter when
body: Integrating third-party or legacy APIs requires changing client code or duplicating translation logic across the system.

title: Trade-off: Adapter
body:
**Benefit**: Enables reuse of existing components without polluting client code.

**Cost**: Adds a translation layer that can hide impedance mismatches or performance costs.

title: Q1: Adapter primarily addresses:
body:
A. Object creation complexity
B. Interface incompatibility between components
C. Concurrent access control
D. State persistence

**B.** It translates one interface into another expected by clients.

title: Q2: In a layered architecture, an adapter commonly lives at:
body:
A. The domain core only
B. An integration boundary such as infrastructure/ports
C. The browser UI exclusively
D. The database index layer

**B.** Adapters bridge external or legacy systems to internal abstractions at boundaries.

title: Intent: Bridge
body: Decouple an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently.

title: Use Bridge when
body: Combining multiple abstractions with multiple implementations via inheritance causes class explosion and tight coupling.

title: Trade-off: Bridge
body:
**Benefit**: Reduces subclass explosion and enables independent evolution of both hierarchies.

**Cost**: Increases design complexity and requires up-front separation of concerns.

title: Q1: Bridge is preferred over inheritance when:
body:
A. Only one implementation will ever exist
B. Two orthogonal dimensions must vary independently
C. Objects must be composed into trees
D. You need to cache remote responses

**B.** It splits abstraction and implementation into separate hierarchies.

title: Q2: A sign Bridge may be missing is:
body:
A. Many subclasses named like FeatureXOnPlatformY
B. Need for undo/redo
C. Expensive object creation
D. Tree traversal requirements

**A.** Combinatorial subclasses indicate abstraction and implementation are tangled.

title: Intent: Builder
body: Separate construction of a complex object from its representation so the same process can create different forms.

title: Use Builder when
body: Creating objects with many optional parts, validation rules, or assembly steps leads to telescoping constructors and fragile setup code.

title: Trade-off: Builder
body:
**Benefit**: Improves readability and correctness for complex object assembly.

**Cost**: Adds classes/objects and can be overkill for simple data structures.

title: Q1: Builder is a better fit than many constructor parameters whe
body:
A. Objects must be globally unique
B. Construction is stepwise with optional parts and validation
C. Behavior must be swapped at runtime
D. Access to a remote service must be proxied

**B.** It makes complex, ordered assembly explicit and safe.

title: Q2: What does a Director contribute?
body:
A. Stores the final product for all clients
B. Encapsulates a reusable construction sequence
C. Selects concrete classes by string name
D. Handles persistence transactions

**B.** The Director knows the order of steps; builders know how to perform each step.

title: Intent: Chain of Responsibility
body: Pass a request along a chain of handlers until one handles or processes it.

title: Use Chain of Responsibility when
body: Coupling senders to specific handlers or writing large conditional dispatch logic makes request processing rigid.

title: Trade-off: Chain of Responsibility
body:
**Benefit**: Decouples senders from receivers and makes pipelines of checks or transforms composable.

**Cost**: A request may go unhandled and chains can be harder to trace.

title: Q1: Chain of Responsibility lets you:
body:
A. Guarantee exactly one handler always runs
B. Decouple sender from the concrete receiver by forwarding along handlers
C. Replicate state across nodes
D. Compile queries into SQL

**B.** Handlers are linked and each decides whether to act or pass along.

title: Q2: A risk to manage in handler chains is:
body:
A. Mandatory global locks
B. Requests falling off the end unhandled
C. Inability to add new handlers
D. Loss of type safety in all languages

**B.** Without a terminal handler or contract, some requests may not be processed.

title: Intent: Command
body: Encapsulate a request as an object, allowing parameterization, queuing, logging, and undo.

title: Use Command when
body: Invokers are tightly coupled to concrete operations, making it hard to queue, audit, retry, or reverse actions.

title: Trade-off: Command
body:
**Benefit**: Decouples invocation from execution and enables scheduling, auditing, and reversal.

**Cost**: Introduces many small command objects and lifecycle management concerns.

title: Q1: Command turns a request into:
body:
A. A database schema
B. A standalone object with execution context
C. A shared mutable singleton
D. A compile-time macro

**B.** Encapsulation as an object enables queuing, logging, and undo.

title: Q2: In CQRS-style systems, commands are useful because:
body:
A. They replace read models entirely
B. They represent intentful writes that can be validated, queued, and audited
C. They guarantee eventual consistency without design
D. They eliminate domain logic

**B.** Commands make write operations explicit and manageable.

title: Intent: Composite
body: Compose objects into tree structures and let clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly.

title: Use Composite when
body: Client code must distinguish leaves from containers when operating over hierarchical structures, leading to special-case logic.

title: Trade-off: Composite
body:
**Benefit**: Simplifies client code and makes it easy to add new component types.

**Cost**: Can make it harder to restrict which children a composite may contain.

title: Q1: Composite is most appropriate for:
body:
A. Flat collections with no nesting
B. Tree-like part-whole structures
C. Request/response retries
D. Two-phase commits

**B.** It models recursive hierarchies behind a uniform interface.

title: Q2: A trade-off of Composite is:
body:
A. Clients must always know concrete types
B. Constraining allowed child types can become harder
C. It cannot support recursion
D. It removes polymorphism

**B.** A uniform component interface can weaken compile-time/type-level constraints.

title: Intent: Decorator
body: Attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it.

title: Use Decorator when
body: Subclassing to add combinations of behaviors (logging, caching, auth, metrics) causes class explosion and rigid composition.

title: Trade-off: Decorator
body:
**Benefit**: Enables flexible, mix-and-match behavior without subclass explosions.

**Cost**: Many small wrappers can complicate debugging and object identity.

title: Q1: Decorator differs from inheritance by:
body:
A. Composing behavior at runtime via wrapping
B. Requiring access to source code
C. Only working for UI widgets
D. Forcing a single global wrapper

**A.** Decorators wrap objects dynamically, allowing flexible combinations.

title: Q2: A common operational pitfall of decorators is:
body:
A. They cannot implement interfaces
B. Wrapper order can change semantics and complicate tracing
C. They require database locks
D. They eliminate the need for testing

**B.** Behavior like auth-before-cache vs cache-before-auth depends on composition order.

title: Intent: Dependency Injection
body: Supply an object’s dependencies from the outside rather than having it construct or locate them internally.

title: Use Dependency Injection when
body: Hard-coded dependencies make code difficult to test, configure, and extend across environments.

title: Trade-off: Dependency Injection
body:
**Benefit**: Improves testability, configurability, and adherence to dependency inversion.

**Cost**: Can obscure object creation flow and introduce container/configuration complexity.

title: Q1: Dependency Injection mainly improves:
body:
A. Network throughput
B. Testability and flexibility by externalizing dependency creation
C. Database normalization
D. Binary size

**B.** Clients receive collaborators, making substitution and configuration easier.

title: Q2: A potential downside of DI containers is:
body:
A. They prevent interface use
B. Wiring can become implicit and harder to trace
C. They require no configuration ever
D. They eliminate constructors

**B.** Automated wiring may hide how objects are composed, so explicitness matters.

title: Intent: Facade
body: Provide a simplified interface to a complex subsystem.

title: Use Facade when
body: Clients must orchestrate many subsystem classes and calls, increasing coupling and misuse risk.

title: Trade-off: Facade
body:
**Benefit**: Reduces coupling and makes common use cases easier and safer.

**Cost**: Can become a god object if it accumulates unrelated responsibilities.

title: Q1: Facade is primarily about:
body:
A. Enforcing one instance globally
B. Simplifying access to a subsystem
C. Sharing intrinsic state efficiently
D. Deferring execution as commands

**B.** It provides a higher-level interface over complex components.

title: Q2: When should clients bypass a facade?
body:
A. Never, facades must hide everything permanently
B. When advanced or uncommon capabilities are legitimately needed
C. Only during testing
D. Whenever performance matters

**B.** Facades simplify common paths but do not have to forbid direct subsystem access.

title: Intent: Factory Method
body: Let subclasses or hook implementations decide which concrete object to create.

title: Use Factory Method when
body: A framework needs to create products while allowing extensions to choose concrete types without changing core workflow code.

title: Trade-off: Factory Method
body:
**Benefit**: Decouples object creation from the high-level algorithm that uses it.

**Cost**: Introduces subclassing or hook points that can proliferate.

title: Q1: Factory Method is most useful when:
body:
A. One global object must be shared
B. Object creation must vary while the workflow stays fixed
C. Multiple objects must be created as a family atomically
D. An object graph is too expensive to copy

**B.** It defers instantiation to an overridable hook so workflows can stay generic.

title: Q2: Compared to putting `if type == ...` in the workflow, Factor
body:
A. Removes all runtime polymorphism
B. Moves variation to a dedicated creation point
C. Requires distributed messaging
D. Eliminates the need for interfaces

**B.** Creation variability is isolated behind the factory method.

title: Intent: Flyweight
body: Share common intrinsic state across many fine-grained objects to reduce memory use.

title: Use Flyweight when
body: Large numbers of similar objects duplicate immutable data, causing high memory overhead.

title: Trade-off: Flyweight
body:
**Benefit**: Reduces memory and allocation costs for large object populations.

**Cost**: Adds complexity and may increase CPU cost to manage extrinsic state.

title: Q1: Flyweight saves memory by:
body:
A. Compressing objects on disk
B. Sharing intrinsic state and externalizing extrinsic state
C. Using lazy database queries
D. Batching network calls

**B.** Common immutable data is stored once and reused across many logical instances.

title: Q2: A precondition for safe Flyweight use is:
body:
A. Intrinsic state must be mutable by clients
B. Clear separation between shared and per-use state
C. All objects must live in one process globally
D. No factory can be used

**B.** Shared state must be immutable or carefully controlled; extrinsic state is supplied per operation.

title: Intent: Iterator
body: Provide a way to access elements of an aggregate sequentially without exposing its representation.

title: Use Iterator when
body: Clients need to traverse collections with different internal structures without depending on their concrete storage details.

title: Trade-off: Iterator
body:
**Benefit**: Simplifies client traversal logic and supports multiple simultaneous traversals.

**Cost**: Adds objects and can be redundant in languages with rich built-in iteration.

title: Q1: Iterator’s key benefit is:
body:
A. Faster sorting algorithms
B. Traversal without exposing internal representation
C. Automatic persistence
D. Distributed consensus

**B.** Clients consume elements through a standard interface regardless of storage layout.

title: Q2: In data pipeline code, iterators are useful because:
body:
A. They eliminate backpressure
B. They provide a uniform way to stream records from varied sources
C. They replace message queues
D. They guarantee exactly-once delivery

**B.** Different sources can expose the same traversal contract to downstream stages.

title: Intent: Mediator
body: Centralize complex interactions between related objects in a mediator to reduce direct dependencies.

title: Use Mediator when
body: Many components reference each other directly, creating tangled communication and fragile change propagation.

title: Trade-off: Mediator
body:
**Benefit**: Reduces coupling between components and localizes collaboration logic.

**Cost**: Mediator can grow into a complex central controller.

title: Q1: Mediator reduces:
body:
A. The need for any interfaces
B. Direct many-to-many dependencies between colleagues
C. All runtime latency
D. Storage requirements

**B.** Peers communicate via a central coordinator rather than referencing each other.

title: Q2: A warning sign when using Mediator is:
body:
A. Colleagues become too reusable
B. The mediator accumulates most business rules and complexity
C. Handlers become stateless
D. Events become immutable

**B.** Centralization helps decoupling but can create a god object if overused.

title: Intent: Memento
body: Capture and externalize an object’s internal state so it can be restored later without violating encapsulation.

title: Use Memento when
body: Implementing undo, checkpoints, or rollback requires access to internal state that should remain private.

title: Trade-off: Memento
body:
**Benefit**: Supports rollback and checkpoints while preserving encapsulation boundaries.

**Cost**: Can consume significant memory or require careful snapshot sizing.

title: Q1: Memento preserves encapsulation by:
body:
A. Making all state public for caretakers
B. Letting the originator create and consume opaque snapshots
C. Storing state only in global variables
D. Serializing directly in every client

**B.** Caretakers hold snapshots without reading their internal structure.

title: Q2: In event-driven systems, mementos are often used for:
body:
A. Routing messages between brokers
B. Checkpointing state for recovery/undo scenarios
C. Load balancing HTTP traffic
D. Schema migration

**B.** Snapshots can complement event streams for rollback or fast restore points.

title: Intent: Observer
body: Define a one-to-many dependency so dependents are notified when a subject changes state.

title: Use Observer when
body: Components need to react to state changes without hard-coded polling or tight coupling between publisher and subscribers.

title: Trade-off: Observer
body:
**Benefit**: Enables loose coupling and dynamic subscription for change propagation.

**Cost**: Notification order, storms, and debugging event flows can be challenging.

title: Q1: Observer is best characterized as:
body:
A. One-to-one synchronous call chains only
B. A publish/subscribe dependency between subject and observers
C. A data partitioning strategy
D. A compile-time code generator

**B.** Observers register interest and receive updates when the subject changes.

title: Q2: In distributed event-driven systems, a common observer risk
body:
A. No way to add subscribers
B. Uncontrolled cascades and unclear delivery/ordering semantics
C. Guaranteed global transactions
D. Static schemas only

**B.** Loose coupling is powerful but requires attention to ordering, retries, and idempotency.

title: Intent: Prototype
body: Create new objects by copying a prototypical instance instead of instantiating from scratch.

title: Use Prototype when
body: Object creation is expensive or configuration-heavy, and new instances should start from known templates with small variations.

title: Trade-off: Prototype
body:
**Benefit**: Speeds creation and centralizes default templates.

**Cost**: Cloning graphs with shared references or cycles can be error-prone.

title: Q1: Prototype is especially helpful when:
body:
A. You need one instance per process
B. Creating from a configured template is cheaper than full construction
C. Objects must never be copied
D. You must enforce access control

**B.** Cloning reuses an initialized template as the starting point.

title: Q2: A key risk with Prototype is:
body:
A. Inability to support interfaces
B. Incorrect deep vs shallow copying of mutable state
C. Guaranteed memory leaks
D. Mandatory network calls during clone

**B.** Copy semantics determine whether clones share nested mutable objects.

title: Intent: Proxy
body: Provide a surrogate or placeholder that controls access to another object.

title: Use Proxy when
body: Direct access to an object is expensive, remote, unsafe, or needs cross-cutting controls like caching or lazy loading.

title: Trade-off: Proxy
body:
**Benefit**: Adds access control or optimization transparently to clients.

**Cost**: Introduces latency/complexity and can obscure failure modes of the real subject.

title: Q1: A proxy and the real subject typically:
body:
A. Expose unrelated interfaces
B. Share the same subject interface so clients are unaware
C. Must run in different processes
D. Cannot be swapped at runtime

**B.** Transparency to the client is a core property of Proxy.

title: Q2: Which is a valid proxy use case?
body:
A. Defining algorithm families
B. Lazy loading or access control around a real object
C. Building objects stepwise
D. Traversing tree structures uniformly

**B.** Proxies control access for concerns like laziness, protection, remoting, or caching.

title: Intent: Repository
body: Mediate between domain and data mapping layers through a collection-like interface for aggregates.

title: Use Repository when
body: Domain logic becomes coupled to queries, ORM APIs, and persistence details, making it hard to test and evolve.

title: Trade-off: Repository
body:
**Benefit**: Improves separation of concerns and testability of domain logic.

**Cost**: Can hide important query capabilities or add leaky abstractions if over-generalized.

title: Q1: Repository aims to present persistence as:
body:
A. A set of HTTP endpoints
B. A collection-like interface over domain aggregates
C. A UI component tree
D. A message broker topic

**B.** It abstracts storage behind domain-oriented operations.

title: Q2: A common repository anti-pattern is:
body:
A. Defining methods per aggregate use case
B. A one-size-fits-all generic CRUD interface that hides important domain queries
C. Using interfaces for testing
D. Separating domain and infrastructure

**B.** Overly generic repositories can leak persistence details or fail to express intent.

title: Intent: State
body: Allow an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes by delegating to state objects.

title: Use State when
body: Behavior that depends on lifecycle state leads to large conditional blocks and invalid transitions scattered through methods.

title: Trade-off: State
body:
**Benefit**: Localizes state-specific behavior and makes transitions explicit.

**Cost**: Increases number of classes and requires careful transition ownership.

title: Q1: State pattern is a strong fit when:
body:
A. Behavior is identical in all modes
B. An object’s behavior and valid transitions depend on lifecycle phase
C. You need to clone object graphs
D. You need a simplified subsystem API

**B.** It encapsulates per-state behavior and transitions.

title: Q2: How does State differ from Strategy conceptually?
body:
A. State is chosen by client only; Strategy never is
B. State transitions are typically driven by context lifecycle, Strategy by interchangeable policy choice
C. State requires databases; Strategy does not
D. They are identical patterns

**B.** Both delegate behavior, but State models internal lifecycle transitions.

title: Intent: Strategy
body: Define interchangeable algorithms behind a stable interface so behavior can vary at runtime.

title: Use Strategy when
body: A service needs multiple pricing, routing, or ranking behaviors without scattering conditionals across callers.

title: Trade-off: Strategy
body:
**Benefit**: Replaces branching logic with composable, testable policies.

**Cost**: Adds indirection and requires explicit strategy selection.

title: Q1: What problem does Strategy primarily solve?
body:
A. Sharing mutable state across objects
B. Selecting algorithms at runtime without caller conditionals
C. Persisting objects to storage
D. Coordinating distributed transactions

**B.** Strategy encapsulates interchangeable behaviors behind a common interface.

title: Q2: In a microservices pricing service, where does Strategy fit
body:
A. As a network retry policy between services
B. As pluggable domain policies inside one service
C. As the service discovery mechanism
D. As the database replication protocol

**B.** It organizes internal behavior variants; cross-service concerns belong to architecture patterns.

title: Intent: Template Method
body: Define the skeleton of an algorithm in a base operation, deferring specific steps to subclasses or hooks.

title: Use Template Method when
body: Multiple implementations share the same overall process but duplicate its structure while varying a few steps.

title: Trade-off: Template Method
body:
**Benefit**: Reuses invariant workflow logic and enforces consistent sequencing.

**Cost**: Relies on inheritance and can make flows harder to follow across class hierarchy.

title: Q1: Template Method centralizes:
body:
A. Object construction of families
B. The invariant sequence of an algorithm
C. Network communication retries
D. Persistent storage schemas

**B.** The base class owns the skeleton; subclasses supply variable steps.

title: Q2: A drawback compared to composition-based alternatives is:
body:
A. It cannot enforce ordering
B. It depends on inheritance, limiting flexibility
C. It prevents code reuse
D. It only works in functional languages

**B.** Behavior variation is expressed through subclassing rather than object composition.

title: Intent: Unit of Work
body: Track changes to objects during a business transaction and coordinate writing them out as a single unit.

title: Use Unit of Work when
body: Multiple repository operations within one use case can become inconsistent without coordinated commit/rollback boundaries.

title: Trade-off: Unit of Work
body:
**Benefit**: Ensures consistency within a transaction and simplifies commit coordination.

**Cost**: Adds complexity and can be awkward across distributed systems or microservice boundaries.

title: Q1: Unit of Work primarily manages:
body:
A. UI rendering state
B. A transactional boundary and tracked changes
C. HTTP routing tables
D. Container orchestration

**B.** It coordinates what must be committed or rolled back as one unit.

title: Q2: Across microservices with separate databases, Unit of Work a
body:
A. Provides global ACID transactions automatically
B. Is limited to local boundaries; sagas/compensation are needed for cross-service consistency
C. Replaces idempotent consumers
D. Eliminates eventual consistency

**B.** Distributed systems require additional coordination patterns beyond a local unit of work.

title: Intent: Visitor
body: Represent an operation to be performed on elements of an object structure without changing the element classes.

title: Use Visitor when
body: Adding new operations across a stable set of element types leads to repeated edits and scattered logic in those classes.

title: Trade-off: Visitor
body:
**Benefit**: Makes adding new operations easy and keeps operation-specific logic cohesive.

**Cost**: Adding new element types requires changing every visitor.

title: Q1: Visitor is a good fit when:
body:
A. Element types change frequently but operations are fixed
B. Element structure is stable and new operations are added often
C. You need to share intrinsic state
D. You need runtime service discovery

**B.** It optimizes for adding operations across a stable set of elements.

title: Q2: A major cost of Visitor is:
body:
A. No way to group operation logic
B. Adding a new element type forces updates to all visitors
C. It cannot traverse structures
D. It requires global variables

**B.** The visitor interface mirrors the element hierarchy.
